# Combining datasets: `join` and `merge` {#sec-m1-joins} Almost no analysis uses a single table. The real work is combining: freight flows with population, highways with municipal GDP, port facilities with IBGE codes. This chapter is about making that combination and, above all, about **finding out what did not match**. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(dplyr) library(stringr) library(readxl) colunas <- c("ano", "perfil", "sh2", "pais_origem", "uf_origem", "cidade_origem", "instalacao_origem", "pais_destino", "uf_destino", "cidade_destino", "instalacao_destino", "tku") cabotagem <- readxl::read_excel("dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.xlsx", na = c("", "-")) stopifnot(ncol(cabotagem) == length(colunas)) names(cabotagem) <- colunas cabotagem <- cabotagem |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.character), str_squish)) |> dplyr::filter(tku > 0) |> dplyr::mutate(uf_origem = stringr::str_to_upper(uf_origem), uf_destino = stringr::str_to_upper(uf_destino), tku_bi = tku / 1e9) nrow(cabotagem) #> [1] 600 ``` ::: ## The types of join We will use two small tables to see how each `join` behaves without noise: flows by destination state (`fluxos`) and GDP by state (`pib`). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fluxos <- data.frame( uf_destino = c("PR", "SP", "BA", "AM"), tku_bi = c(4.8, 12.3, 3.1, 0.4) ) pib <- data.frame( uf = c("PR", "SP", "BA", "CE"), pib_bi = c(613, 2720, 400, 220) ) ``` ::: ### `left_join()`: keeps the left table This is what you will use in 90% of cases: it keeps every row of the main dataset and brings in the columns of the auxiliary one. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fluxos |> dplyr::left_join(pib, by = c("uf_destino" = "uf")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: `AM` got `NA` because it does not exist in the GDP table. **That is information**, not an error. And it must be investigated, never ignored. ### `inner_join()`: only what exists in both ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fluxos |> dplyr::inner_join(pib, by = c("uf_destino" = "uf")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: Careful: `inner_join` **silently drops rows**. Always compare `nrow()` before and after. ### `full_join()`: the union ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fluxos |> dplyr::full_join(pib, by = c("uf_destino" = "uf")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ### `anti_join()` and `semi_join()`: the diagnostic tools ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # what is in the flows and has NO GDP fluxos |> dplyr::anti_join(pib, by = c("uf_destino" = "uf")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # what is in the GDP table and does not appear in the flows pib |> dplyr::anti_join(fluxos, by = c("uf" = "uf_destino")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # filters the flows, keeping only those with a match in GDP (without bringing columns) fluxos |> dplyr::semi_join(pib, by = c("uf_destino" = "uf")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## The routine that prevents errors when combining Always, in this order: 1. `anti_join()` in both directions, to see what does not match. 2. `left_join()`. 3. Check `nrow()` before and after. If it grew, the key on the right is duplicated. 4. Count the `NA`s in the columns brought in. ::: ### Summary table | Function | Rows kept | Typical use | |:--|:--|:--| | `left_join()` | all from the left | add attributes to the main dataset | | `inner_join()` | only those that match | when the analysis needs both pieces of information | | `full_join()` | all from both | consolidate complementary datasets | | `anti_join()` | left without a match | **diagnosing** keys that do not match | | `semi_join()` | left with a match | filter by a list of codes | The base R equivalent is `merge()`, with the arguments `all.x`, `all.y`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} merge(fluxos, pib, by.x = "uf_destino", by.y = "uf", all.x = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ## The row duplication problem If the key of the right-hand table has repeated values, the `join` **multiplies** the rows. It is the most common cause of inflated totals in reports. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pib_dup <- dplyr::bind_rows(pib, data.frame(uf = "PR", pib_bi = 999)) nrow(fluxos) #> [1] 4 fluxos |> dplyr::left_join(pib_dup, by = c("uf_destino" = "uf")) |> nrow() #> [1] 5 ``` ::: Modern `dplyr` warns you about this if you declare the expected relationship: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fluxos |> dplyr::left_join(pib_dup, by = c("uf_destino" = "uf"), relationship = "one-to-one") #> Error in `dplyr::left_join()`: #> ! Each row in `x` must match at most 1 row in `y`. #> ℹ Row 1 of `x` matches multiple rows in `y`. ``` ::: Declaring `relationship = "one-to-one"` (or `"many-to-one"`) turns a silent error into an explicit one. It is worth always using it in production routines. ## Fixing data before merging In practice, the problem is never the `join`. It is the key. Four fixes solve almost everything. ### 1. Different type ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} a <- data.frame(cod = c("4118204", "3548500"), valor = c(10, 20)) b <- data.frame(cod = c(4118204, 3548500), pop = c(156174, 418375)) class(a$cod); class(b$cod) #> [1] "character" #> [1] "numeric" ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dplyr::left_join(a, b, by = "cod") #> Error in `dplyr::left_join()`: #> ! Can't join `x$cod` with `y$cod` due to incompatible types. #> ℹ `x$cod` is a . #> ℹ `y$cod` is a . ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dplyr::left_join(a, dplyr::mutate(b, cod = as.character(cod)), by = "cod") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ### 2. Lost leading zero State, municipality and census tract codes read as numbers lose the leading zero. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} codigos <- c(1100015, 110001) stringr::str_pad(codigos, width = 7, pad = "0") #> [1] "1100015" "0110001" ``` ::: ### 3. Case, accents and spaces ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chave <- function(x) { x |> stringr::str_squish() |> stringr::str_to_lower() |> stringi::stri_trans_general("Latin-ASCII") } x <- data.frame(municipio = c("São Gonçalo do Amarante", "Paranaguá")) y <- data.frame(municipio = c("SAO GONCALO DO AMARANTE", "PARANAGUA"), pop = c(104669, 156174)) dplyr::left_join( dplyr::mutate(x, k = chave(municipio)), dplyr::mutate(y, k = chave(municipio)) |> dplyr::select(-municipio), by = "k" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ### 4. Composite key A municipality name is only unique **within** its state. That is why the correct key is `municipality + state`. Better still: the IBGE code. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bonitos <- data.frame( municipio = c("Bonito", "Bonito", "Bonito"), uf = c("MS", "PA", "PE") ) area <- data.frame( municipio = c("Bonito", "Bonito", "Bonito"), uf = c("MS", "PA", "PE"), area_km2 = c(4934, 1789, 395) ) dplyr::left_join(bonitos, area, by = c("municipio", "uf")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-important} ## Always use the IBGE code when it exists The 7-digit code (`4118204` = Paranaguá/PR) is the official key and does not suffer from the problems above. In module 2, `geobr::read_municipality()` brings this code together with the geometry, and in module 3 `censobr` and `sidrar` use it as the identifier. Keep it in every intermediate table you create. ::: ## Application: enriching the coastal shipping dataset Let us add the **region** of origin and of destination to the flows, using an auxiliary table of states. Before the `left_join`, the diagnosis. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} regioes <- data.frame( uf = c("AC","AL","AP","AM","BA","CE","DF","ES","GO","MA","MT","MS","MG","PA", "PB","PR","PE","PI","RJ","RN","RS","RO","RR","SC","SP","SE","TO"), regiao = c("Norte","Nordeste","Norte","Norte","Nordeste","Nordeste","Centro-Oeste", "Sudeste","Centro-Oeste","Nordeste","Centro-Oeste","Centro-Oeste","Sudeste", "Norte","Nordeste","Sul","Nordeste","Nordeste","Sudeste","Nordeste","Sul", "Norte","Norte","Sul","Sudeste","Nordeste","Norte") ) # 1. what does not match, in both directions cabotagem |> dplyr::anti_join(regioes, by = c("uf_origem" = "uf")) |> dplyr::count(uf_origem, wt = tku_bi, name = "tku_bi") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cabotagem |> dplyr::anti_join(regioes, by = c("uf_destino" = "uf")) |> nrow() #> [1] 0 ``` ::: The diagnosis found what we already knew from @sec-m1-limpeza: the origin may be the **ZEE/Continental Shelf** or **Indeterminado** (undetermined), which are not states. And they account for a huge share of the TKU. An `inner_join` here would erase almost 40% of the data without warning. The solution is to extend the auxiliary table to hold these categories explicitly: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} regioes <- dplyr::bind_rows( regioes, data.frame(uf = c("ZEE/PLAT. CONTINENTAL", "INDETERMINADO"), regiao = c("Offshore (ZEE)", "Indeterminado")) ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} n_antes <- nrow(cabotagem) cabotagem_reg <- cabotagem |> dplyr::left_join(regioes, by = c("uf_origem" = "uf"), relationship = "many-to-one") |> dplyr::rename(regiao_origem = regiao) |> dplyr::left_join(regioes, by = c("uf_destino" = "uf"), relationship = "many-to-one") |> dplyr::rename(regiao_destino = regiao) # 3. the rows did not multiply c(antes = n_antes, depois = nrow(cabotagem_reg)) #> antes depois #> 600 600 # 4. no NA left in the columns brought in c(origem = sum(is.na(cabotagem_reg$regiao_origem)), destino = sum(is.na(cabotagem_reg$regiao_destino))) #> origem destino #> 0 0 ``` ::: The join is validated. Now the matrix of flows between regions, in billions of t·km (the regions are North, Northeast, Centre-West, Southeast and South): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cabotagem_reg |> dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku_bi), .by = c(regiao_origem, regiao_destino)) |> tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = regiao_destino, values_from = tku_bi, values_fill = 0) |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 1))) |> dplyr::arrange(regiao_origem) |> knitr::kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |regiao_origem | Sul| Nordeste| Sudeste| Norte| |:--------------|----:|--------:|-------:|-----:| |Indeterminado | 0.0| 0.0| 0.0| 0.0| |Nordeste | 5.6| 8.9| 18.8| 10.9| |Norte | 4.0| 27.3| 15.8| 10.5| |Offshore (ZEE) | 16.5| 23.2| 69.8| 0.0| |Sudeste | 5.7| 21.5| 5.7| 18.6| |Sul | 0.9| 15.8| 0.9| 6.6| ::: ::: Reading this table answers a planning question in a few lines: the largest flows are **offshore to the Southeast** (about 70 billion t·km), followed by **North to Northeast** and **offshore to the Northeast**. In other words: oil from the platforms to the terminals in the Southeast and Northeast, and container cargo leaving Manaus. ### Stacking instead of joining When the tables have the same structure (for example, one file per year), the operation is `bind_rows()`, not `join`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} anos <- 2020:2025 arquivos <- sprintf("dados/cabotagem_%d.xlsx", anos) serie <- lapply(arquivos, read_excel) |> dplyr::bind_rows(.id = "i") |> dplyr::mutate(ano = anos[as.integer(i)]) |> dplyr::select(-i) ``` ::: `bind_rows()` aligns the columns by name and fills with `NA` those missing in some file. It is desirable behaviour, but it hides a column being renamed between years. Check with `setdiff(names(a), names(b))` before stacking.
